title: The Evolution of Growing Season Thirstwave Characteristics Across the CONUS From Historical to Future Climate Conditions
abstract: Thirstwaves are a recently identified meteorological phenomenon characterized by prolonged periods of anomalously high atmospheric evaporative demand. They are defined as periods of at least three consecutive days during which reference short crop evapotranspiration (ETos) exceeds a day-specific 90th-percentile threshold. Unlike temperature- or precipitation-based metrics, ETos integrates the combined effects of temperature, humidity, wind speed, radiation, and atmospheric pressure, providing a standardized measure of atmospheric water demand. Here, we investigate how thirstwave frequency, duration, and intensity may change across the contiguous United States (CONUS) under future climate conditions. Daily ETos was calculated from meteorological output from the 80-member Community Earth System Model Version 2 (CESM2) Large Ensemble for a historical period (1850-2014) and a future SSP3-7.0 scenario (2015-2100). Thirstwaves were identified throughout the CONUS during April-October using grid-point-specific 90th-percentile ETos thresholds derived from a 15-day moving climatological window. Future characteristics were evaluated relative to the historical climatology. Results indicate substantial increases in thirstwave characteristics across much of the CONUS, with frequency, duration, and intensity exhibiting distinct spatial responses. The Northeast and Southwest exhibit the largest increases in thirstwave frequency and duration, while the Midwest experiences the greatest increases in thirstwave intensity. Despite relatively modest changes in the mean characteristics of thirstwaves, their future distributions shift substantially toward more frequent and intense extremes. These results indicate that extreme atmospheric water demand may become increasingly common and severe throughout the twenty-first century, with potential implications for agricultural water demand, water resources, and ecosystem resilience.

title: 1.6 - It's Not Just the Storm: Understanding Escalating Severe Convective Storm Losses
abstract:
Severe convective storms (SCSs) have emerged as one of the most consequential sources of insured weather loss in the United States, with recent years characterized by increasingly frequent multibillion-dollar loss events. The causes of this trend, however, are often reduced to changes in the physical hazard itself, particularly those associated with climate change. While an evolving SCS hazard landscape is an important component of changing risk, economic losses ultimately arise from the intersection of the hazard with a much broader and dynamically changing set of societal and economic conditions.

Here, we introduce an ingredients-based framework for understanding escalating SCS losses. Analogous to ingredients-based approaches used in weather forecasting (Doswell et al. 1996), the framework considers loss as the product of several interacting components: hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and economic and policy conditions. Changes in the frequency, intensity, location, or seasonality of SCS hazards can alter physical risk, but these changes occur simultaneously with population growth and migration, expansion of the built environment, increasing property values, changes in construction and housing characteristics, inflation in materials and labor, supply-chain constraints, insurance and regulatory practices, and other factors affecting the cost of damage and recovery. Importantly, these ingredients do not operate independently; their overlap can compound losses, while dependencies among them can generate cascading economic consequences extending well beyond the immediate storm footprint.

We use the rapidly growing SCS loss burden as a case study to demonstrate why attribution of loss trends requires integration of atmospheric science, catastrophe modeling, economics, engineering, insurance, and social sciences. The framework provides a common conceptual language for separating—and ultimately quantifying—the contributions of physical hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and economic change. We conclude by identifying key observational, modeling, and interdisciplinary research needs required to better diagnose historical loss trends, anticipate future SCS risk, and translate weather and climate science into more effective decisions across the insurance, policy, and resilience communities.

Doswell, C. A., III, H. E. Brooks, and R. A. Maddox, 1996: Flash flood forecasting: An ingredients-based methodology. Wea. Forecasting, 11, 560–581, https://doi.org/10.1175/1520-0434(1996)011<0560:FFFAIB>2.0.CO;2

title: 2.1 - Constructing Severe Convective Storm Event Sets using GCM and Reanalysis-Derived Environments Using Machine Learning
abstract: Robust characterization of severe convective storm (SCS) risk under present and future climates requires a large and physically consistent event set that adequately sample the tails of environmental distributions. Traditional approaches using SCS reports are limited by the relatively short observational record and/or the computational expense of convection-allowing simulations. This work introduces a scalable framework for generating large event sets of SCS-favorable environments using bias-corrected output from the Community Earth System Model (CESM). We train machine learning models on reanalysis-derived environmental fields with target outputs defined by practically perfect hindcasts of severe weather occurrence. This approach enables the identification of environmental patterns most strongly associated with observed severe convective hazards. The trained models are then applied to bias-corrected CESM simulations to diagnose SCS-relevant environments across a substantially larger sample space than is available from reanalysis alone. To further enhance sampling of extreme, but plausible, environments, stochastic techniques are employed to perturb and augment the CESM-derived event set, preserving key multivariate dependencies while expanding representation of low-probability, high-impact scenarios. The resulting dataset provides a physically grounded and computationally efficient means of generating large ensembles of severe storm environments suitable for risk assessment, catastrophe modeling, and climate change attribution studies.

title: 3.1 - Keynote Speaker Victor Gensini: Translating Severe Convective Storm Science into Actionable Risk
abstract:
Severe convective storms (SCSs)—including large hail, tornadoes, and damaging straight-line winds—generate persistent and highly volatile losses for insurers, reinsurers, property owners, and communities. SCS losses emerge from the intersection of hazard, exposure, vulnerability, and human behavior, each of which is evolving on different spatial and temporal scales. Consequently, increasing losses cannot be attributed to a single cause, and historical loss experience alone may not adequately represent future risk.

This keynote will examine the current scientific understanding of severe convective storm risk and its application to insurance and financial decision-making. Topics will include the strengths and limitations of historical storm reports, radar-derived climatologies, environmental proxies, machine-learning methods, and convection-permitting climate simulations. Particular attention will be given to the spatial and seasonal variability of hail, tornado, and wind hazards; the challenge of representing localized and tail-risk events; and the evidence for, and uncertainty surrounding, changes in severe convective storm environments under a warming climate.

Drawing upon research and industry engagement through the Center for Interdisciplinary Research on Convective Storms (CIRCS), the keynote will conclude with pathways of collaboration among atmospheric scientists, catastrophe modelers, insurers, reinsurers, engineers, and public-sector partners. Such collaboration is essential for converting improved understanding of storms into more credible risk estimates and more resilient communities.

title: 3.3 - Identifying Sources of Kelvin Wave Forecast Errors: A Baroclinic Mode Analysis of MPAS-A Simulations
abstract:
Accurately predicting convectively coupled Kelvin waves (CCKWs) remains a major challenge for numerical models. Improving these forecasts is critical, as CCKWs strongly modulate tropical weather and trigger extreme events like tropical cyclogenesis. To investigate the root causes of CCKW forecast deficiencies, we evaluate Model for Prediction Across Scales – Atmosphere (MPAS-A) experiments at both parameterized (15–30 km) and convection-permitting (3 km) resolutions. These simulations are run with different convective schemes and initial CCKW amplitude perturbations. An object-tracking analysis reveals that parameterized MPAS-A simulations produce CCKWs that decay and propagate too quickly, echoing known biases in operational systems. Furthermore, artificially amplifying the initial CCKW yields only temporary skill improvements. These findings suggest that CCKW forecast errors stem primarily from model deficiencies in representing CCKW growth processes, rather than flawed initial conditions.

To diagnose the physical drivers of under-amplified CCKW growth, we decompose the wave's vertical structure into baroclinic modes using empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs). This isolates the wave-damping impacts of deep convection (EOF1) and the growth impacts of stratiform heating (EOF2). We find that the MPAS models often produce excessively damped first modes (EOF1) and fail to fully capture the covariance between temperature and diabatic heating in the second vertical mode (EOF2). Because this second mode is essential for wave amplification, its deficiency helps explain CCKW forecast errors. Ultimately, advancing CCKW forecasts requires better representing deep convection and stratiform-driven wave growth. We also argue that data-driven forecast models and machine learning postprocessing offer promising pathways to improve CCKW predictions.

title: Torque Contributions to Atmospheric Angular Momentum Tendency During the Madden-Julian Oscillation
abstract: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) is associated with intraseasonal variability of atmospheric angular momentum (AAM), a global measure of large-scale circulation variability; however, the evolution of AAM and the contributions of torques across the MJO life cycle have not yet been quantified. Global relative AAM tendency is calculated from ERA5 (1940–2025) to produce phase aware lag-lead composites, allowing for characterization of relationships between MJO phase evolution, AAM tendency, and friction, mountain, gravity wave drag, and Coriolis torques. We find coherent phase lag structure within approximately 10 days of MJO phase occurrence and opposing MJO phases associated with opposite signed AAM tendency anomalies. Friction and mountain torques represent the largest contributors to the composite torque signal with their relative contributions varying across MJO phase and lag. There is robust seasonal variation in the strength and coherence of AAM, torque, and MJO relationships, with larger signals during boreal spring and summer. This work quantifies the close association between global momentum exchange and MJO evolution, identifying the torque pathways associated with intraseasonal AAM variability. Ongoing analysis examines the spatial circulation and torque structures underlying these relationships as well as implications for tropical-extratropical interaction on subseasonal timescales.

title: Using Score-Based Diffusion to Emulate Precipitation from a Convection-Permitting Regional Climate Model
abstract: Dynamical downscaling has improved the representation of precipitation and organized convection (e.g., supercells and mesoscale convective systems) but remains computationally expensive. To address these limitations, recent advances in deep learning, particularly score-based diffusion models, offer stable training and high-fidelity generation of gridded climate fields. Additionally, diffusion models have enabled kilometer-scale generative downscaling at a fraction of the computational cost of dynamical downscaling while preserving realistic spatial structure and intensity distributions of target atmospheric phenomena. This study applies a generative score-based diffusion framework for emulating precipitation at convection-permitting scales. Predictor data are derived from the ~100-km bias-corrected Community Earth System Model (CESM), whereas the target consists of 6-h accumulated precipitation from a 3.75-km horizontal grid spacing convection-permitting simulation. NVIDIA’s CorrDiff model is adapted to this application and trained on the existing dynamically downscaled dataset to generate ensembles of high-resolution precipitation. Water years (WY) 1990–2005 from the target historical simulation are divided into training (WY 1990–1999), validation (WY 2000–2001), and testing (WY 2002–2005) datasets. The approach is evaluated using metrics and diagnostics of performance and fidelity across the spectrum of precipitation intensity and coverage. Early results indicate that the CorrDiff diffusion step can reproduce precipitation structure and intensity across a range of spatial scales, with improved Fractions Skill Score (FSS) and power spectral density (PSD) characteristics relative to the deterministic baseline. A fully validated emulation framework could offer a more efficient way to generate ensembles of high-resolution realizations and to characterize uncertainty.

title: 1C.5 - Assessment of Precipitation Morphology in Climate Model Realizations Downscaled Using Residual Corrective Diffusion
abstract:
Organized deep, moist convection (DMC) can produce dangerous lightning, flash flooding, damaging wind, large hail, and tornadoes. Despite their societal importance, there is a limited understanding of how anthropogenic climate change might influence the spatiotemporal frequency of these events. Existing work using GCMs suggests some regions may experience more days with large-scale environments that are conditionally favorable for organized DMC. However, important mesoscale processes, including convective initiation and storm organization, are not resolved by GCMs. Dynamical downscaling addresses this limitation by using GCM output to drive a convection-permitting RCM that explicitly resolves mesoscale processes. However, this improvement comes with a significant computational cost. The WRF BCC dataset is a recent example of this approach, using a target horizontal grid spacing of 3.75 km and a temporal resolution of 15 minutes. Creating this ~1 PB dataset required ~107 core hours on high-performance computing clusters, limiting the feasibility of generating large ensembles of high-resolution realizations needed to characterize uncertainty.

Recently, generative machine learning approaches such as residual corrective diffusion, including NVIDIA’s CorrDiff, have been developed to emulate convection-permitting RCMs by generating high-resolution realizations directly from coarse-resolution predictors such as GCM fields. These approaches can reproduce mesoscale features at a greatly reduced computational cost. This work extends ongoing evaluations of CorrDiff by assessing the morphology of 6-h precipitation depicted in large ensembles of generatively downscaled climate realizations. An adapted CorrDiff model was trained using hundreds of predictor variables from a bias-corrected version of CESM1 (CMIP5), with historical 6-h precipitation accumulation (1990 – 2005) from a convection-permitting WRF-ARW simulation as target data. Related ongoing work has demonstrated that the best performing model markedly improves the bulk accuracy of the predictions in the diffusion step relative to the initial regression prediction.

To evaluate whether these improvements extend to organized DMC structures, a precipitation morphology classification model is applied to both target and generated fields to identify pertinent precipitation morphologies, including isolated cells and mesoscale convective systems. The generated realizations include many of the structures represented in the target data. However, the performance varies by region, synoptic regime, and season. The results demonstrate that generative diffusion can produce physically meaningful precipitation structures similar to convection-permitting simulations, while also identifying cases where the generative model needs improvement. Overall, this approach warrants further examination, particularly for applications requiring large ensembles of high-resolution climate fields.

title: 9A.2 - Extreme Precipitation Associated with Quasi-Linear Convective Systems over the Central and Eastern Conterminous United States under Intermediate and Pessimistic Climate Change Scenarios
abstract: Quasi-linear convective systems (QLCSs) have pronounced impacts on the hydroclimate of the conterminous United States east of the Rocky Mountains (ECONUS) and contribute to hydrological hazards such as flash flooding, which cause immense economic losses and can pose a substantial threat to life. Furthermore, anthropogenic climate change may influence these systems in various ways, including regional reduction or intensification of short-duration, high-intensity precipitation, potentially increasing the societal impacts of these events. However, few studies have examined potential future ECONUS spatiotemporal changes to hourly extreme precipitation (EP) produced by QLCSs. This study analyzes changes in hourly EP produced by QLCSs over the ECONUS, using convection-permitting, dynamically downscaled regional climate model output for three 15-year epochs. These epochs include a historical baseline (HIST; 1990–2005) and two end-of-21st-century periods (END; 2085–2100) under either an intermediate (END4.5) or pessimistic (END8.5) representative concentration pathway (RCP). An updated segmentation, tracking, and identification machine learning method identifies QLCS events across epochs, which are spatiotemporally compared to hourly EP occurrences. Results suggest that overall mesoscale convective system-associated EPs (MEPs) will become more frequent east of the Mississippi River under both future climate scenarios, with the largest increases in spring and fall. Decreases in MEP days are projected over the summer, primarily in the Great Plains. Regional analysis highlights the Northeast as most likely to be affected by changes in MEPs, with significant increases across all four seasons. Largely driven by increases in MEPs, EP frequency is also projected to increase in future climates east of the Mississippi River. Overall, this research provides insight for forecasters, stakeholders, and the public into how these events may change and, moreover, inform resilient measures to mitigate and adapt to precipitation-based hazards.

title: A Climatology of Supercells in the United States Using Dynamically Downscaled Simulation Output
abstract:
Supercells produce a majority of the significant tornadoes and hail in the United States and account for a disproportionate share of severe convective storm losses. Existing supercell climatologies and future projections are generally based on 10–15-year periods, limiting the ability to distinguish long-term trends from interannual and interdecadal variability. This study develops a supercell census spanning more than four decades using the CONUS404 dataset. Simulated supercells are identified using 2–5-km AGL updraft helicity and tracked hourly across the eastern contiguous United States, producing a catalog sufficient to resolve variability across annual to multidecadal timescales.


The historical climatology reproduces established spatial patterns in U.S. supercell occurrence while revealing notable regional differences in storm frequency, intensity, size, and longevity. Supercell occurrence increases by a net 19.4% between 1980-2024, although substantial interannual and interdecadal variability complicates the long-term signal. The Great Plains exhibit the historical maximum in simulated supercell activity, with a mean annual occurrence of approximately 314.3 supercells. Seasonally, the Southern Plains and Southeast exhibit peaks in simulated supercell activity during MAM, while the Midwest and Northern Plains peak during JJA. Diurnal variability is also evident, with supercell initiation peaking between 23Z and 02Z across most regions. The Northeast is the primary exception, with initiation peaking near 21Z.

title: The Role of Extratropical Cyclones In a Changing Severe Convective Storm Climatology
abstract: Severe convective storms (SCS) cause billions of dollars in damage across the contiguous United States (CONUS) each year and are frequently associated with extratropical cyclones (ETCs), whose warm sectors provide the thermodynamic and kinematic environments favorable for deep, moist convection. Although research has examined changes in SCS environments and peril reports over time, comparatively little work has directly examined ETC and their affiliated SCS environments have changed or will change in the future. The goal of this study is to generate a climatology of ETCs across the central and eastern CONUS and, thereafter, develop an understanding of the efficiency of SCS environments affiliated with these ETCs in the production of SCS perils. Using CONUS404 and ERA5 output, an automated tracking framework for ETCs is developed to provide details on cyclone evolution, trajectory, and intensity for a historical period. Favorable SCS environments are evaluated using thermodynamic, kinematic, and composite SCS parameters, permitting ETCs to be categorized according to the magnitude and spatial extent of the SCS-favorable environment within and near their warm sectors. These implicit environmental characteristics will then be compared with explicit peril proxies from CONUS404 to examine changes in the relationship between ETC environments and SCS production over a 40-year historical period and, time and data permitting, a future climate scenario. The hypothesis is that changes in ETC characteristics contribute to observed and projected future shifts in the climatology of favorable SCS environments and their realizations. This framework will help clarify the extent to which changes in SCS climatology are linked to changes in ETC characteristics, the environments they support, and their ability to produce perils.

title: Understanding the Hydration of the Upper Troposphere and Lower Stratosphere by Tropical Cyclone
abstract: A cooling trend in the tropical lower stratosphere represents one of the most significant climate signals in recent records. Recent evidence suggests that these stratospheric temperature variations have contributed significantly to the interannual variability of TC potential intensity over the last three decades. Despite these findings, the extent of stratosphere-troposphere exchange (STE) and contribution within a TCs remains uncertain. Observations and numerical simulations have shown the impact of TCs intensity on the magnitude and vertical distribution of water vapor change at upper levels. While observations and numerical modeling have demonstrated that TC intensity affects the magnitude and vertical distribution of upper-level water vapor, high-resolution idealized frameworks evaluating UTLS thermodynamic controls remain limited. This study utilizes idealized Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model simulations to isolate the impact of UTLS temperature variations on TC intensity and subsequent lower stratospheric hydration. Results demonstrate that variation in UTLS temperature impacts the TC intensity, which significantly influences lower stratospheric hydration levels, with stronger cyclones leading to a greater moisture influx into UTLS. Stronger tropical cyclones generate a more extensive hydration layer with dehydration zone as is observed in previous studies, whereas weaker TCs show no significant hydration layer was produced. Further, results show that UTLS hydration varies distinctively between the inner core and outer rainbands, jointly driven by TC intensity and differences in tropopause height and temperature.
